About: Thermal Expansion — the Hole Gets Bigger Too

Source

Topic
Thermal properties of matter (Class 11)
Concept
Every linear dimension of a heated solid scales by (1 + αΔT), including lengths measured across empty space — so a hole in a plate gets bigger, not smaller.
Serves
JEE / NCERT Class 11 — linear, areal and volumetric expansion; expansion of cavities.
Inquiry
What does the hole do as the plate is heated — shrink, stay the same, or grow?
Misconception
“The expanding metal closes the hole.” No: every distance scales together.

Thermal Expansion
Three expansions, one ΔT — ghost outline = cold metal
Cold (ghost)
Hot

Guided Inquiry

Predict: what does the hole do?

A steel ball sits stuck on a metal ring — the ball is 0.030 mm wider than the cold hole. You are about to heat the ring. Commit to a prediction first: as the ring heats up, the hole will…

Heat it — free the ball.

Drag ΔT up slowly and watch the middle panel: the true clearance creeps from negative toward zero… and the ball drops through. The pass/fail moment uses the real micrometre numbers, not the drawing scale.

Meanwhile the rail on the left eats into its expansion gap. Push ΔT far enough and the gap closes — the rail buckles. That gap is exactly why rails and bridges are built with one.

The 1 : 2 : 3 ratio, live.

Watch the three strain bars along the bottom while you drag ΔT: length, area and volume strains grow together, always in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3. Switch material — the bars rescale but the ratio never changes.

That is because (1 + αΔT)² − 1 ≈ 2αΔT and (1 + αΔT)³ − 1 ≈ 3αΔT to first order. Try Invar: α is so small the ball never drops.

Why the hole grew.

Pick any two points of the cold ring — one on each side of the hole. After heating, every distance between two points of the metal is multiplied by (1 + αΔT), including the one measured across the empty gap.

So the hot ring is a photographic enlargement of the cold ring. The hole grows by the same fractional amount as a solid disc of the same material would — which is why heating a stuck jar lid loosens it.

01

At a glance

One temperature slider heats three metal parts at once: a railway rail, a ring with a ball resting on it, and a cube. The sim lets you read off what the heat does to each part, in real millimetres.

What you'll learn

  • How a solid's change in length, area and volume depends on the temperature rise ΔT and the material's coefficient α.
  • How the size of a hole cut in a plate responds to heating.
  • Why rails and bridges are laid with a gap, and how to test a fit in micrometres.
The three parts. Each starts at the same temperature and is heated by the same ΔT.

What's on screen

  • Left panel: a 1 m rail held between two anchors with a 1.0 mm gap, and the label ΔL.
  • Middle panel: a ball resting on a plate with a round hole. The label gives the ball, hole and clearance in millimetres.
  • Right panel: a cube, with its cold outline dashed behind it.
  • Strain bars (bottom): three bars labelled ΔL/L₀, ΔA/A₀ and ΔV/V₀.
See itStart with the steel parts at ΔT = 50 K and a 20 mm hole. Watch for: the ball resting on the plate with the label stuck, ball wider than the hole.

03

Every length in a heated solid scales by the same factor

A length L₀ in a solid grows to L when the temperature rises by ΔT, where α is the material's linear expansion coefficient:

ΔL = L₀ α ΔT, L = L₀(1 + α ΔT)
The change is a fixed fraction αΔT of the length you started with.

This holds for any length in the solid, including one measured across empty space. Pick two points of the cold ring on opposite sides of the hole: the distance between them is multiplied by (1 + αΔT) like every other distance. So the hole diameter follows d = d₀(1 + αΔT), and the hot ring is a scaled-up copy of the cold one.

For steel (α = 12 × 10⁻⁶ /K), ΔT = 50 K and d₀ = 20 mm, αΔT = 0.060 %, so the diameter changes by 20 mm × 0.00060 = 0.012 mm.

See itHeat the steel ring by ΔT = 50 K. Watch for: the readout Hole diameter change +0.0120 mm and the label under the ring, hole 20.012 mm.
04

A hole grows enough to release the ball

The ball is 0.030 mm wider than the cold hole, so it rests on the ring until the hole is at least as wide as the ball. The diameter must grow by 0.030 mm, which needs

d₀ α ΔT ≥ 0.030 mm
A bigger hole, a bigger α or a bigger ΔT each helps.
  • Steel with d₀ = 20 mm needs ΔT of about 125 K. Aluminium needs about 63 K.
  • Steel with d₀ = 40 mm needs only about 63 K, because the same fraction is taken of a longer length.
  • The sim decides pass or fail from the true numbers. The picture exaggerates the clearance ×900 so that micrometres are visible.
See itHeat the steel ring by ΔT = 150 K with a 20 mm hole. Watch for: the ball dropping through, and the label clearance +6 µm (true).
05

Area and volume follow from length

An area is a length times a length, and a volume is a length cubed. When every length is multiplied by (1 + αΔT), the area is multiplied by (1 + αΔT)² and the volume by (1 + αΔT)³. Because αΔT is tiny, these are very nearly

ΔA/A₀ ≈ 2αΔT, ΔV/V₀ ≈ 3αΔT
The area coefficient is β ≈ 2α and the volume coefficient is γ ≈ 3α.

So the three fractional changes grow in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3. For steel at ΔT = 50 K the bars read 0.060 %, 0.120 % and 0.180 %. The approximation drops terms such as (αΔT)². At the sim's extreme, aluminium at 200 K, the exact area change is 0.962 % against the 0.960 % the bar shows.

See itHeat aluminium by ΔT = 200 K. Watch for: the three bars reading 0.480 %, 0.960 % and 1.440 %.
06

A rail needs an expansion gap

The 1 m rail lengthens by ΔL = L₀αΔT with L₀ = 1 m. With steel at ΔT = 50 K that is 0.600 mm, which uses up 0.600 mm of the 1.0 mm gap and leaves 0.40 mm. Once ΔL passes 1.0 mm the rail has nowhere to go and the sim draws it buckling.

Materialα (10⁻⁶ /K)gap closes at ΔT
Aluminium24about 42 K
Copper17about 59 K
Steel12about 83 K
Invar0.52000 K, out of the sim's range
See itHeat the steel rail by ΔT = 100 K. Watch for: ΔL = 1.200 mm in the rail's label and the red warning gap closed, the rail buckles.
07

Where it matters

  • Shrink fits. A metal ring is heated until its hole is wider than a shaft, slipped on, and left to cool. As it cools its hole shrinks back and grips the shaft.
  • Expansion joints. Rails, bridges and long pipes are laid with gaps or sliding joints so that a summer rise in temperature has room to act.
  • Stuck lids. Hot water on a metal jar lid enlarges the lid more than the glass beneath, which loosens it.
  • Low-α alloys. Invar's α is 24 times smaller than steel's in the sim, so it suits parts whose size must hold steady as the temperature changes.
08

Summary

In one line. How much a heated solid changes in length, area and volume is set by the temperature rise ΔT and the coefficient α of its material.

Key points

  • Every length, a hole's diameter included, changes by L₀αΔT.
  • Area changes by about 2αΔT and volume by about 3αΔT, as fractions.
  • A fit passes when d₀αΔT is at least the clearance it needs.

Common mix-ups

  • "The metal swells inward, so the hole closes." The distance across the hole scales like any other distance, so the hole gets bigger.
  • "A 20 mm hole and a 40 mm hole grow by the same amount." They grow by the same fraction, so the 40 mm hole grows twice as many millimetres.
  • "The area changes by αΔT." That is the change in length. The area changes by about twice as much.

Things to try on your own

  • With steel and a 40 mm hole, find the smallest ΔT at which the ball drops, and compare it with 0.030 ÷ (40 × 12 × 10⁻⁶).
  • Set ΔT to 200 K and compare the rail's ΔL for steel and for Invar.
  • Find the smallest hole diameter, in whole millimetres, for which aluminium at ΔT = 200 K releases the ball.
